analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $6.65 an hour and indexes it to inflation.
analysis.headline: A minimum wage bill backed by 108 House members never got a committee vote and died without reaching the House floor at the end of 1998.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise the federal minimum wage in three annual steps — to $5.65 in September 1998, $6.15 in 1999, and $6.65 in 2000 — and then automatically adjust it each year for inflation starting in 2001. The indexing provision means Congress would never again have to vote to raise the wage; it would rise with the cost of living on its own. The bill was introduced in January 1998, referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, sent to a subcommittee two weeks later, and never received any further action before that Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, who would see their hourly pay rise by $1.50 over three years and then keep pace with inflation automatically. Most minimum wage workers are adults in food service, retail, and care work, and many support families.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers paid at or near minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum wage from its then-current level of $5.15 to $6.65 an hour by September 2000, a roughly 29% increase spread over three years [S2][S3].

Beginning September 1, 2001, the Secretary of Labor must adjust the wage each year to match increases in the Consumer Price Index, so the wage floor keeps pace with the cost of living without requiring new legislation [S3].
The increases take effect September 1, 1998, so the first raise would come within months of the bill's introduction [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay low wages — concentrated in restaurants, retail, and other service industries — would bear the direct cost of higher payroll, with some of it likely passed to consumers through prices. An indexed wage also removes the periodic bargaining over tax offsets that businesses used in past minimum wage negotiations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: A 29% increase in the wage floor over three years would raise costs most sharply for small businesses and labor-intensive employers like restaurants, which an honest supporter has to acknowledge; opponents of past increases argued this can reduce entry-level jobs or hours, though the evidence on modest increases is disputed.

Automatic inflation indexing cuts both ways: it protects workers' pay in good years, but it also locks the wage at whatever level it reaches, even in a recession, with no chance for Congress to reassess — a design cost a supporter would concede.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a guaranteed, inflation-proof raise of $1.50 an hour for the lowest-paid workers — a large, certain gain for millions of households. The cost falls on low-wage employers and, partly, on consumers through prices, with the main risk being reduced entry-level hiring. Because the increases were phased over three years and the indexing clause made the wage self-sustaining, this was a straightforward, well-designed wage floor bill; the design tradeoffs (fixed indexing, no small-business carve-outs) are real but modest relative to the direct gains for workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee and then in a subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken on it before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. David Bonior, the House Democratic Whip, introduced the bill on January 27, 1998, with roughly 83 original cosponsors listed in the bill text [S3].
It attracted 107 cosponsors — 106 House Democrats and 1 Independent — but no Republicans [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction, and on February 13, 1998 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections [S5].
No further action was recorded: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that pay the minimum wage — restaurants and retail chains most of all — were better off because the bill died: the federal wage floor stayed at $5.15 an hour, and no inflation indexing was ever put in place, so workers had to wait for Congress to raise the wage again.

sides.party_line_note: All 107 cosponsors were House Democrats except one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The industry is the largest employer of minimum wage workers and would have absorbed the largest payroll increase, rising to $6.65 an hour by 2000 with automatic annual increases thereafter. Its interest in keeping the wage floor at $5.15 ran directly against the pay of the workers it employs.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: These employers would have faced the same stepped increases and permanent inflation indexing, removing their leverage in future wage negotiations. Their cost is the workers' gain in this bill.
Not an industry, but a concentrated beneficiary group: the bill's raises and indexing provision would have delivered a guaranteed pay increase to workers at the bottom of the wage scale.
